## Motivation and setup

Radio astronomy offers a way to study astronomical objects beyond visible light, but the equipment can appear inaccessible to an undergraduate laboratory or amateur group. This project develops an affordable experiment from commercially available satellite-television components. Its aim is educational as well as observational: to connect receiving electronics, digitization, calibration, statistical noise, and astronomical interpretation in a working instrument.

The telescope operates near 11.2 GHz. A parabolic dish concentrates incoming radiation onto a low-noise block receiver, or LNB. A satellite finder acts as a square-law detector, producing a signal related to received intensity. An Arduino Uno digitizes the output with a ten-bit analog-to-digital converter at ten samples per second. A set-top box supplies power, and a Python pipeline records and displays the measurements. The instrument measures the total received intensity across its operating band, connecting changes in detector voltage to sources crossing the antenna beam.

![Figure 1. Block diagram of the radio-telescope setup. ([arXiv:1601.02982](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.02982))](../assets/papers/1601.02982/setup_circuit.png){fig-alt="block diagram of the radio-telescope setup, showing the antenna and receiver, satellite finder, power supply, digitization, and computer."}

The Sun supplies a strong first target. Geostationary satellites provide reference signals for calibration, and sky observations away from a target supply the background. Pointing is manual, using predicted altitude and azimuth. For satellite calibration, rotating the LNB aligns its receiving element with the transmitted polarization and maximizes the detected signal. The resulting voltage change provides a direct demonstration of the receiver’s polarization response.

The calibration begins with the Friis transmission relation:

$$
\frac{P_r}{P_t}=G_tG_r\left(\frac{\lambda}{4\pi R}\right)^2.
$$

Here the received and transmitted powers are $P_r$ and $P_t$, the antenna gains are $G_r$ and $G_t$, $R$ is the satellite distance, and $\lambda$ is the observing wavelength. Satellite equivalent isotropically radiated power combines the transmitter power and gain, allowing the received reference power to be estimated from accessible satellite information.
:::

::: {.summary-section}
## Construction and main results

Converting a voltage change into an astronomical measurement requires both the detector calibration and an estimate of the effective collecting area. The receiving gain is related to dish diameter and aperture efficiency by

$$
G_r=\eta_A\left(\frac{\pi d}{\lambda}\right)^2.
$$

The aperture efficiency $\eta_A$ accounts for the difference between geometric dish area and effective collecting area. The calibration uses this information to turn the measured satellite voltage above background into a power scale. The solar signal is then calibrated relative to the satellite observation, preferably taken close in time so that instrumental conditions are comparable.

A drift scan holds the antenna pointing fixed while the sky moves through its beam. Fitting the solar transit with a Gaussian provides a beam-width estimate as well as a recognizable source detection. The paper reports beam widths of approximately $3.4$–$3.5$ degrees, with the tabulated fits giving $3.357\pm0.021$ and $3.501\pm0.007$ degrees. These measurements agree with the approximate beam width expected for the instrument. The broad beam makes source acquisition forgiving, while also limiting angular resolution.

![Figure 2. Drift scan of the Sun. Cyan points show the data, and the black line is a Gaussian fit. ([arXiv:1601.02982](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.02982))](../assets/papers/1601.02982/pp.svg){fig-alt="solar drift-scan plot, with cyan measured points and a black Gaussian fit used to estimate the antenna beam width."}

The received power is then converted to flux density, including the single-polarization response and the difference between the satellite's transmitted bandwidth and the receiver's solar-observation bandwidth. Dividing the flux by the solar solid angle gives intensity. Assuming thermal radiation in the Rayleigh–Jeans regime, the corresponding brightness temperature is

$$
T=\frac{I\lambda^2}{2K_B}=10078\,K.
$$

Here $I$ is the inferred intensity, $K_B$ is Boltzmann's constant, and the numerical value follows from the measured solar signal in the worked calibration. The two reported solar brightness temperatures are 10078 K and 10136 K, with quoted uncertainties of 295 K and 324 K. Brightness temperature expresses the observed radio intensity as the temperature of a thermal emitter at the operating frequency, characterizing the Sun's microwave emission.

Sensitivity can improve by averaging longer. The radiometer equation gives the dependence on averaging time and bandwidth:

$$
\sigma_T\propto\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau\Delta\nu_{RF}}}.
$$

The output fluctuation $\sigma_T$ decreases as integration time $\tau$ or receiver bandwidth $\Delta\nu_{RF}$ increases, under the assumptions behind that noise model. Increasing integration from one second to sixty seconds enabled the reported drift-scan detections of Saturn and a Galactic-arm crossing. The Saturn detection has a reported signal-to-noise ratio of three, with transit timing checked against the predicted sky motion.
:::

::: {.summary-section}
## Noise, calibration, and an undergraduate experiment

The instrument connects several normally separate classroom topics in one measurement. The receiving chain illustrates amplification and detection; the digitizer turns a continuous voltage into a sampled series; calibration connects the output to physical units; and drift scans relate time-domain structure to the motion of the sky. Strong satellite signals make it practical to explore alignment, polarization, and gain before turning to astronomical targets. The Sun then supplies a bright extended source whose transit measures the antenna response.

Characterizing noise is part of this experimental chain. Comparing ordinary sky measurements with measurements taken while the LNB is shielded identifies features generated within the receiving system. Fourier analysis shows a feature around half a hertz that appears in both sets of measurements. This common structure helps connect the measured time series to the electronics and separates different contributions to the output fluctuations.

The surrounding temperature also tracks the detector voltage, with a reported correlation coefficient of 0.98. Measuring that dependence provides a practical introduction to instrumental drift and explains the value of satellite calibration close in time to a solar scan. The temperature conversion combines an assumed aperture efficiency, satellite reference powers, the measured voltage above background, and a bandwidth correction appropriate to broadband solar emission. Each step gives a physical meaning to a quantity that begins as a detector reading.

For weaker sources, the broad receiver bandwidth and longer integration supply the sensitivity gain described by the radiometer relation. The reported Saturn signal, with a signal-to-noise ratio of three, and the Galactic-arm crossing are identified by comparing the measured transit times with the predicted field of view. This ties the observing geometry to the statistical interpretation of the data and makes background measurements central to source identification.

The resulting experiment offers a compact route from commercially available receiving hardware to a calibrated view of the radio sky. It supports exercises in beam-width measurement, flux calibration, thermal-radiation analysis, time-series statistics, and observational planning. Changes in integration time and pointing let students test how the instrument responds, while the acquisition and visualization pipeline makes the connection between hardware settings and measured signals immediately accessible.
